subject: anatomy
title: Pleural Cavity, Costodiaphragmatic Recesses, and Bronchopulmonary Segments

steps.tx: The pleura is a closed serous sac invaginated by the lung, comprising an inner visceral pleura intimately adherent to the lung parenchyma and an outer parietal pleura lining the thoracic cage. Between these layers lies the **pleural cavity**, containing a thin film of lubricating serous fluid that eliminates respiratory friction.
steps.say: The pleura forms a closed serous sac with inner visceral and outer parietal layers. Between them lies the pleural cavity, filled with a thin fluid film that eliminates friction during respiration.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic comparing visceral and parietal pleural reflections at the 6th, 8th, 10th, and 12th ribs
vis.caption: Parietal and visceral pleural reflection levels across the midclavicular, midaxillary, and scapular lines. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The parietal pleura is subdivided into four anatomical regions: cervical pleura (cupola) capping the lung apex, costal pleura lining the ribs, diaphragmatic pleura covering the diaphragm, and **mediastinal pleura** bounding the lateral mediastinum. Only the parietal pleura is innervated by somatic nerves (intercostal and phrenic), perceiving sharp localized pain.
steps.say: The parietal pleura is divided into cervical, costal, diaphragmatic, and mediastinal regions. Innervated by somatic intercostal and phrenic nerves, only the parietal pleura generates sharp localized pain.

left.title: Parietal Pleura
points: Innervated by intercostal and phrenic nerves
Costal pleura pain refers to chest wall
Central diaphragmatic pain refers to C4 shoulder tip

right.title: Visceral Pleura
points: Autonomic visceral afferents: insensitive to pain
Responds only to stretch or ischemia

steps.tx: Potential spaces where opposing surfaces of parietal pleura come into direct contact are termed **pleural recesses**. The largest is the slit-like costodiaphragmatic recess, located along the inferior thoracic margin between costal and diaphragmatic pleurae. During deep inspiration, the expanding inferior lung borders descend into this reserve space.
steps.say: Pleural recesses are reserve spaces where opposing parietal layers meet. The largest is the costodiaphragmatic recess, an inferior slit into which the lung borders descend during deep inspiration.

Clear on normal cross-sectional chest imaging

steps.tx: Surface markings of the lung and parietal pleura follow the classic symmetrical **two-rib rule**. In the midclavicular, midaxillary, and scapular lines, the inferior border of the lung lies at ribs six, eight, and ten, respectively; whereas the inferior reflection of the parietal pleura lies two ribs lower at ribs eight, ten, and twelve.
steps.say: Surface projections of lung and pleura follow the two-rib rule. In midclavicular, midaxillary, and scapular lines, the lung rests at ribs six, eight, and ten, while the pleura extends two ribs lower to ribs eight, ten, and twelve.

steps.tx: Because the **costodiaphragmatic recess** forms the most dependent gutter of the pleural space, pleural effusions, hemothoraces, and empyemas collect here first. On an upright posteroanterior chest radiograph, blunting of the sharp costophrenic angle indicates the accumulation of at least two hundred milliliters of pleural fluid.
steps.say: As the lowest gutter of the pleural cavity, fluid collects first in the costodiaphragmatic recess. On an erect radiograph, blunting of the sharp costophrenic angle indicates at least two hundred milliliters of fluid.

vis.alt: Erect chest radiograph demonstrating dense pleural effusion blunting the costodiaphragmatic angle
vis.caption: Erect posteroanterior chest radiograph demonstrating massive pleural effusion and costophrenic blunting. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The right lung is divided into three lobes by two fissures: an **oblique fissure** separating the inferior lobe from superior and middle lobes, and a horizontal fissure separating superior and middle lobes. The left lung is divided into only two lobes by a single oblique fissure, featuring an anterior cardiac notch and lingula.
steps.say: The right lung is split into three lobes by oblique and horizontal fissures. The left lung has two lobes divided by a single oblique fissure, featuring a cardiac notch and lingula.

points: Horizontal fissure (4th costal cartilage to oblique)

steps.tx: A **bronchopulmonary segment** is the anatomically and functionally independent surgical unit of the lung. Each segment is aerated by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus and supplied by a segmental branch of the pulmonary artery running centrally, while intersegmental pulmonary veins travel in the peripheral connective tissue septa.
steps.say: A bronchopulmonary segment is the independent surgical subunit of the lung. Each segment is aerated by a tertiary bronchus and central pulmonary artery branch, while pulmonary veins travel peripherally between segments.

nodes.label: Segmental Bronchus and Pulmonary Artery Branch Run Together Centrally
Pyramidal Lung Segment Base at Pleura, Apex at Hilum
Intersegmental Pulmonary Veins Course in Peripheral Septa
Enables Anatomical Segmentectomy without Damaging Adjacent Segments

steps.tx: At the **pulmonary hilum**, structures entering and exiting the lung are enclosed by a reflection of pleura that hangs downward as the pulmonary ligament. In the right hilum, the eparterial bronchus lies most superiorly above the pulmonary artery; in the left hilum, the pulmonary artery is most superior above the single left main bronchus.
steps.say: At the lung hilum, entering vessels and airways are enveloped by pleura forming the inferior pulmonary ligament. In the right hilum, the eparterial bronchus sits above the pulmonary artery; in the left, the artery sits on top.

rows: Most inferior vascular exit in both hila
